text: - Renewed consideration be given to establishing a permanent police presence in Fregon that would consist of officers residing in and being stationed at Fregon. Response of the South Australian Government This recommendation is not supported. •   South Australia Police (SAPOL) has been reviewing staffing and infrastructure for the APY Lands since late 2019 and has considered options for providing a police presence in Fregon. SAPOL has developed a proposed new staffing model to enhance service provision across the APY Lands, including the Fregon community. SAPOL is also investing approximately $1.5 million in a new facility in Fregon (subject to tender processes) to support the new staffing model and policing presence. This will enable police patrols to spend more time in the community and stay overnight as required. SAPOL has also undertaken a high-level scoping exercise to establish the requirements necessary to provide a 24/7 full time policing presence as recommended by the inquest. At this time, the new proposed staffing model, along with enhanced (short stay capable) police facilities in the Fregon community will be implemented as soon as possible and the impact in terms of these changes on service delivery to the Fregon community will be monitored.

- The Attorney-General introduce legislation to amend Part 3, Division 5 of the Sentencing Act 2017 to impose obligations upon SAPOL, the Department for Correctional Services and the Parole Board in appropriate cases to advise the Attorney-General that a particular prisoner should be considered as the possible 20 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court subject of an application to the Supreme Court pursuant to section 57 of the Sentencing Act 2017 for an order that the prisoner be detained in custody until further order. Response of the South Australian Government This recommendation is supported in principle. •   A key finding of the Deputy State Coroner was that, while Mr Davey had a long, frequent and serious criminal history (including sexual offending) that commenced as a juvenile, he was not on parole or under any supervision at the time he abducted and murdered Mrs Woodford. One of the issues considered by the Deputy State Coroner was whether, before Mr Davey’s ultimate release, and prior to the expiration of his sentence, an application could have been made by the Attorney-General for Mr Davey to be kept in custody for an indeterminate period of time pursuant to section 23 of the repealed Criminal Law (Sentencing) Act 1988, now section 57 of the Sentencing Act 2017. While the Deputy State Coroner made no finding as to whether the application should have been made by the Attorney-General, he was critical of the fact that it was not brought to the Attorney-General’s attention that Mr Davey could have been the subject of an application under section 23. There is currently no legislative obligation requiring relevant agencies to advise the Attorney-General that a particular prisoner should be considered as the possible subject of an application. The Attorney-General’s Department will progress amendments to Part 3, Division 5 of the Sentencing Act 2017 to impose obligations upon SAPOL, DCS and the Parole Board, to advise the Attorney-General that particular prisoners should be considered as the possible subject of an application to the Supreme Court pursuant to section 57. - Relevant staff of the Department for Correctional Services should be reminded of the terms of DCS Local Operating Procedure entitled ‘Oversight of Prisoners pursuant to section 23 of the Criminal Law (Sentencing) Act 1998’ (or its current version) relating to serious repeat sexual offenders constituting a high risk and of the obligations contained within that document concerning the operation of section 57 of the Sentencing Act 2017. Response of the South Australian Government This recommendation is supported. A comprehensive review of processes associated with section 57 of the Sentencing Act 2017 across DCS has been undertaken, including revising the existing Local Operating Procedure (LOP). The revised LOP was circulated internally on 18 June 2021. 21 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Following the LOP revision, consideration was given to incorporating the relevant processes within a DCS Standard Operating Procedure (SOP). DCS considers this process will have a stronger effect than merely reminding staff of the existing LOP via a Chief Executive Instruction. A draft SOP has now been prepared for review. It will be published for consultation in mid-September 2021 and then implemented by the end of October 2021. In the interim, DCS is confident that the revised LOP provides appropriate instruction to relevant staff.

- That in any review of the operation of relevant provisions of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (South Australia) Act 2010 and the Regulations made thereunder as they apply to health practitioners providing services in remote areas of South Australia, that consideration be given to clarifying whether the requirements in respect of a second responder should apply to presentations by a patient to the home of the health practitioner. The other matter that should be considered in any such review is whether health practitioners should be accompanied by the second responder during any journey to the location where the health service is to be provided. Response of the South Australian Government This recommendation is supported. •   In 2017, in response to the death of Mrs Woodford, the South Australian Parliament passed the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (South Australia) (Remote Area Attendance) Amendment Act, more commonly referred to as ‘Gayle’s Law’. The Act came into operation on 1 July 2019, and requires health service providers that employ health practitioners in remote areas to ensure a second responder accompanies any health practitioner who attends an out of hours or unscheduled callout. A mandated review of Gayle’s Law was near completion at the time of the Deputy Coroner handing down his findings into the death of Mrs Woodford. Professor Robyn Aitken of Flinders University led the review and gave consideration to the Coroner’s findings in the formulation of her report. Professor Aitken’s report was tabled in Parliament on 27 May 2021. The report aligns with the Deputy Coroner’s recommendations, and further recommends that Gayle’s Law be extended to preclude the delivery of health care at the home of a health practitioner or second responder at any time of day or night (beyond out of hours and unscheduled callouts).1 In addition, the report recommends that amendments should be made to section 77E(2) of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (South Australia) Act 2010 to ensure that health practitioners are always accompanied by a second responder during the journey to all callout locations.2 SA Health will lead a broad consultation to ensure that any proposed amendments to the legislation and regulations are considered in consultation with all stakeholders. - The State Government consult with APY communities and relevant authorities concerning implementation of measures regarding the release of offenders at high risk of serious offending to the APY Lands, such measures to include the precluding of such an offender from residing on the APY Lands, the placement of conditions on the offender if residing on the APY Lands and the provision of advice to service providers on the APY Lands in respect of the offender and the risk of reoffending identified by the authorities. Response of the South Australian Government This recommendation is supported. •   The Criminal Law (High Risk Offenders) Act 2015 (CLHRO Act) provides for the ongoing supervision of certain offenders beyond the expiry of any term of imprisonment or parole. Under the CLHRO Act, an Extended Supervision Order (ESO) may be made for a period of up to five years. 22 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Section 11 of the CLHRO Act provides that the Parole Board may impose various conditions on an ESO, including requiring the offender to reside at a specified address, or to prohibit or restrict an offender from residing or being present at, or in the vicinity of, a specified place or premises, or a place or premises of a specific class, for example, the APY Lands. To date, no offenders subject to an ESO have been permitted to reside in the APY Lands. ESOs cannot be effectively supervised on the APY Lands for several reasons, including: •    the unreliability of GPS signal required for electronic monitoring •    the lack of supervision resources •    limited access to support services and intervention Consultation under this recommendation will address what measures need to be considered with respect to offenders at a high risk of serious offending who may not be captured by the CLHRO Act. Initial multi-agency consultation has commenced with the APY Lands Executive Board with regard to this recommendation. - That the Department for Correctional Services and the South Australian Prison Health Service revise procedures relating to the transfer of prisoners from one DCS institution to another DCS institution, which revised procedures should contain the following elements: a.   There should be a formal handover from the HRAT at the transferring institution to the HRAT at the receiving institution. The handover should be conducted by the respective Managers of Offender Development. The handover should identify any recommendations that have been made within DCS and SAPHS as to the accommodation of the prisoner in the receiving institution. The handover should also identify the reason or reasons for the transfer and in particular whether it involves the need for a medical or psychiatric evaluation of the prisoner at the receiving institution. There should be an automatic take-up of the prisoner’s HRAT regime at the receiving institution without the need for the raising of a fresh NOC. b.   There should be a formal handover as between DCS staff at the transferring institution and the DCS staff at the receiving institution. The handover should involve a formal communication between the General Managers of both institutions or as between their designated delegates. c.   There should be a formal handover as between the SAPHS staff at the transferring institution and the SAPHS staff at the receiving institution. Responses from the Department for Correctional Services •    DCS has recently reviewed and enhanced its processes for managing prisoners at risk of suicide and self- harm, including a review of Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 090, Management of Prisoners at Risk of Suicide or Self-Harm (SOP 90). The revised SOP 90 was fully implemented in 2019. A High Risk Assessment Team (HRAT) operates within each prison. Prisoners who are assessed to be at risk of suicide and/or self-harm are monitored through the HRAT multi-disciplinary team process. The HRAT process also provides intervention and support to such prisoners. Prisoners placed under the supervision of the HRAT are discussed at weekly HRAT forums. These multi- disciplinary forums include representatives from SAPHS, the Department’s Statewide Operations – Offender Services branch, social workers, Aboriginal Liaison Officers (ALOs) and psychologists.

- That the Department for Correctional Services implement more effective measures to ensure that prisoners under a HRAT regime and who therefore should not be left alone in cells during lockdown periods are not left alone in those periods, such measures to include: a.   The use of electronic monitors within the staff offices of each accommodation unit that display a live list of prisoners accommodated within the particular unit who are the subject of HRAT monitoring. Responses from the Department for Correctional Services •    The officer station board lists all prisoners in each unit, with those prisoners on HRAT highlighted, this is considered to be a ‘live list’ (and is often referred to as count boards). In addition, the Department has made changes to the Justice Information System (JIS) that now identify that a prisoner is currently subject to HRAT monitoring. The HRAT flag on the JIS has been made more visible to staff members and is clearly visible across a number of JIS screens. Whilst an active HRAT flag is removed once the prisoner is removed from HRAT monitoring, the inactive flag will remain on the JIS Warning screen, indicating that the prisoner has previously been subject to HRAT monitoring and the dates that they were subject to that monitoring in the past. This serves as a visual reminder of historical ‘at risk’ periods. These changes were implemented and fully operationalised by DCS on 10 December 2018. b.   That DCS staff be obliged to endorse a document in respect of each HRAT prisoner whenever the HRAT prisoner is locked down, the endorsement to acknowledge that the DCS officer is satisfied that the HRAT prisoner has not been left in the cell on his or her own. Responses from the Department for Correctional Services •    When a prisoner subject to HRAT monitoring is required to be placed in a ‘double cell’, the cell must be occupied by a second prisoner at all times. When prisoners are secured within the cell, arrangements must be made to ensure the HRAT prisoner’s safety should the second prisoner be absent from the cell for an extended period of time (e.g. overnight, to attend court, to attend a medical appointment). - I direct this recommendation to the Minister for Health, the Minister for Correctional Services, the Chief Executive of the Department for Correctional Services and the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service. a.   I recommend that close attention should be given to the opinions of Dr Narian Nambiar, the Clinical Director of the Statewide Forensic Mental Health Service, as expressed in his oral evidence given to the Court in this matter. In particular I recommend the establishment of a prison ‘In-reach team’ to be operated by the Statewide Forensic Mental Health Services. The In-reach team would comprise the following elements: •    Nursing staff who are qualified mental health nurses and who actually work in the prison and who are able to triage and provide mental health assessments of prisoners on an ongoing basis. •    Video link assessments in respect of prisoners who are situated outside the metropolitan area. •    Consultation as between members of the In-reach team and a prisoner’s family, especially an Aboriginal prisoner’s family, concerning the prisoner’s history and presentation and other relevant matters. 27 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •   A multi-disciplinary approach to the care of mental health patients in the prison system, such an approach being provided by nursing staff, psychologists and social workers, and in the case of Aboriginal prisoners, Aboriginal Liaison Officers. Mental Health services are provided to prisoners under DHW by the FMHS through the Northern Adelaide Local Health Network (NALHN). - This recommendation is directed to the attention of the Minister for Health, the Minister for Correctional Services, the Chief Executive of the Department for Correctional Services and the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service. a.     I recommend that consideration be given to an amendment to the Mental Health Act 2009 in respect of the imposition of inpatient treatment orders on persons in DCS custody. In his evidence Dr Nambiar agreed with the observation that certain elements of the operation of the Mental Health Act are inappropriate in a consideration as to whether or not an inpatient treatment order should be imposed under the Mental Health Act on a prisoner. In this regard it will be remembered that guiding principal 7(1)(b) in the Act asserts that mental health care should be provided in the least restrictive way and in the least restrictive environment that is consistent with the efficacy of the mental health services to be engaged and with public safety. An inpatient treatment order which involves the detention of a person under the Act may only be imposed where there is no less restrictive means than an inpatient treatment order of ensuring appropriate treatment of a person’s illness.13 Less restrictive means than the imposition of an inpatient treatment order would include a community treatment order. It is at least questionable as to whether a community treatment order can effectively be imposed on a person already in custody. If anything, the least restrictive environment for a detained prisoner would involve detention under the Act as distinct from custody in the general prison population. The other relevant matter as pointed out to the Court by Mr Homburg, counsel for Dr Nambiar, is that a structural obstacle for the treatment of mentally ill prisoners is the absence of any recognition in the Mental Health Act of the reality faced by all prisoners, namely, the absence of their liberty to choose when and how to seek psychiatric care. Mr Homburg exemplifies this by pointing out that prisoners restricted in their ability to attend medical appointments or to voluntarily present at an emergency department when an acute need arises. Mr Homburg argues that the objects of the Mental Health Act do not conform with the reality that is faced by people who are incarcerated. He points out that the Mental Health Act is predicated on an expectation that persons to whom the Act might apply are capable of retaining freedom rights. He argues that it is very difficult to achieve all of the Act’s objectives and to satisfy its guidelines where an individual whose liberty is already restricted needs to be considered for detention under the Act. In my opinion there is much force in those submissions.

- SA Health continue to implement and action the recommendations of the Chief Psychiatrist as described within the Action Plan in Response to the Investigation Report of the Chief Psychiatrist, with the only modification being that emphasis should be placed on the need for continuing professional development of rural general practitioners in relation to mental health care as distinct from the credentialing of those practitioners; Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions taken by the OCP as detailed: •   SA Health are continuing to implement and action the recommendations of the Action Plan in response to the investigation report of the Chief Psychiatrist. This will be monitored. •   Regional Mental Health Services have addressed four of these seven recommendations: progression to a single clinical record remains ongoing; education and training modules for GPs has been funded, developed 30 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court and field tested; the final rollout is now occurring, and this will allow recommendation six to move from credentialling’ to continuing professional development. •   The modification suggested by the Coroner to extend this to CPD is accepted. Work is currently underway to review existing CPD in this area for GPs.

- A comprehensive review be conducted in relation to clinical resources in respect of mental health services in all rural regions in South Australia. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions taken by the OCP as detailed: •   The review has been commissioned by the Minister. •   Arrangements are currently being confirmed. The Terms of Reference implement these Coroner’s Recommendations. •   Continuity of care is a consideration given by clinicians throughout a person’s journey within the health system and plays an important role in assisting in therapeutic engagement with the individual in care. It is also dependent on good systems and procedures and having the appropriate resources to implement those systems and procedures. A review of the services will assist in determining where gaps may exist and what changes may need to be implemented to improve continuity of care in regional services. •   Regional hospitals with a designated mental health unit were gazetted on 5 June 2017 to be Approved Treatment Centres and could then maintain a person on a Level 2 or 3 Inpatient Treatment Order (ITO). Prior to that date, they were Limited Treatment Centres and were restricted to a person being subject to a Level 1 ITO only. The Terms of Reference for the Review consider the capability of hospitals to implement this.

- I recommend that psychiatrists and other practitioners and clinicians who practise in rural areas be advised of, or be reminded of, the following: •   That purely cross-sectional analyses of patients presenting with mental illness or possible mental illness should be avoided. •   That there is a need to examine the longitudinal history of the presenting patient. •   That there is a need to gather collateral information from family members and associates of the presenting patient. The need for the gathering of collateral information has been a repeated theme in a number of coronial inquests. A similar need was identified in the inquest of Noakes. •   That there is a need to evaluate and identify a deterioration in the mental health of a patient from one presentation to the next. •   That in particular cases there may be a need for general practitioners practising in rural hospitals to utilise the services of Emergency Triage Liaison Service. •   That there is a need for psychiatric evaluation of a patient who makes repeated presentations. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been accepted and response incorporates actions taken by the OCP as detailed: •   A notice to all staff has been prepared by the OCP and will be sent to all mental health clinicians to remind them of these requirements. •   It is also noted that, all clinicians in mental health are expected to use assessments that include a consideration of a person’s longitudinal history and the need for obtaining collateral information is well understood. •   All services have procedures related to deteriorating mental state as required in the National Safety and Quality Health Services Standards: Recognising and Responding to Acute Deterioration Standard 8. 31 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •   Staff and other interested parties, including GPs and non-government health service providers, have access to education programs related to suicide prevention including mental health assessments, suicide prevention

- I recommend that except in relation to electro-convulsive therapy and neurosurgery, the relevant provisions of the Mental Health Act 2009 be amended by deleting as a requirement for the imposition of any level of Inpatient Treatment Order or Community Treatment Order that the person in question has impaired decision-making capacity relating to appropriate treatment of the person’s mental illness. Response from SA Health The recommendation has been noted and response from the OCP as detailed: •   The Mental Health Act will be reviewed in 2022 by the South Australian Law Reform Institute. The recommendation will be considered in the review of the Mental Health Act 2009 due to be undertaken in 2022 and the impact this may have on the rights of a person with a mental illness under national and international agreements and obligations. •   The inclusion of mental capacity and impaired decision making in relation to the making of a Mental Health Legal Order (MHLO) was included in the Mental Health Act 2009 (the Act) from June 2017. •   This recommendation has been included in the Terms of Reference for the Act Review. Stachor, Joshua Marek (Coroner White) Before making these recommendations, I acknowledge that many of these endorse recommendations made by this Court on previous occasions, in particular by Deputy State Coroner Schapel in his findings in the Blunden Inquest. The Court makes the following recommendations directed to the attention of the Minister for Correctional Services, the Chief Executive of the Department for Correctional Services, the Minister for Health, the Chief Executive of SA Health and the Commissioner of Police.

- That the Department for Correctional Services continue to identify and eliminate hanging points from cells in all South Australian correctional facilities. Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   With respect to potential ligature (hanging) points, the Department continues to modify infrastructure to remove or modify potential points based on an assessment of risk. DCS’ Policy 39 Prioritisation for Implementing Safe Cells was developed and endorsed by Executive in August 2014. The purpose of the policy is to classify cells across the system pursuant to Policy 39, Prioritisation for Implementing Safe Cells, and to identify and prioritise a schedule of works that ensure the identified highest risk areas are targeted first. The following principles form the basis of Safe Cell design: •      No obvious hanging or ligature points; •      Forced air circulation throughout all cells; •      All edges are rounded; •      All knobs/taps are sloped; •      Safety screws used throughout; •      Wall fixtures sit flush with walls; •      All joins are sealed; and 32 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court •    All lighting is recessed or anti-ligature in design. The current status of safe cells in DCS is as follows: •    All newly constructed secure custody cells meet ‘safe cell’ specifications. •    DCS over a number of years, has been installing furniture and cell fixtures, which comply with safe cell design guidelines in order to reduce the potential for prisoner self-harm. •    Ongoing works through future annual capital works programs continue to reduce the ability for self-harm

- That the Chief Executive of the Department for Correctional Services takes steps to identify and appoint correctional officers who are specifically dedicated to the task of admitting prisoners to correctional institutions in South Australia. These dedicated correctional officers should be thoroughly trained in all aspects of the admission process. They should also be thoroughly trained in the use of the Justice Information System and should have full and unrestricted access to the information contained on that system including, but not limited to, information about the admitted prisoner that has previously been placed on the Offender Casenotes by DCS staff and members of the HRAT. Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   DCS operates on rotating rosters and at this time, the recommendation to identify and appoint correctional officers who are specifically dedicated to the task of admitting prisoners to correctional institutions is not consistent with operational practices. However, steps taken to consolidate the skills amongst targeted groups of staff at larger institutions include: •    Admission roles being part of one roster so the same staff rotate through the roles and not all staff; •    The Adelaide Remand Centre (ARC) being designated as the state’s primary admissions facility, with YLP no longer taking admissions; •    Staff who work admissions at the ARC are all on one roster rather than all staff cycling through admission positions which further develops skills and expertise. All staff involved in the prisoner admission process are thoroughly trained in all aspects of the admission process and the requirements under Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 001A Case Management – Custodial Admission (SOP 001A), and SOP 090, Management of Prisoners at Risk of Suicide or Self-Harm (SOP 090). These staff use and have full access to information on the electronic Justice Information System (JIS), including the prisoners historical HRAT information.

- That the officers who specialise in admissions be subject to continuing education and training relevant to their work. This scheme would involve a mandatory number of hours of continuing education per calendar year to be eligible to continue in the role. Training should incorporate concentration on Notices of Concern and the duties involved in understanding operating procedures regarding admissions and raising Notices of Concern. It should also cover education on the basics of mental health afflictions and common physical signs of mental health problems. 33 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   DCS has recently established a Mandatory Training team who will oversee the co-ordination of the delivery of staff mandatory training. There is no on-going formal training for officers provided by the Correctional Officer Training Course once graduated, however on 3 November 2021 a ‘Mandatory Training Alert’ announcement was electronically distributed to all DCS staff advising of an e-Learning package on SOP 090. This e-Learning package is aimed at all Correctional Officers (CO2 to CO7) and staff working with prisoners in a correctional setting and is required to be completed every three years. From 1 April 2022, staff working in admissions must be current in the SOP 090 e-learning to undertake the admissions role. Suicide Awareness and Self Harm training is currently provided to DCS correctional staff, facilitated face to face by Lifeline. Additionally, all officers undergo training in Mental Health and Suicide awareness, which is to be completed every three years. Trainee Correctional Officers (TCOs) have a two-hour training session on SOP 090 which includes completing a NOC, which is covered in multiple sessions such as suicide awareness and mental health awareness. - That the admission documents for a prisoner must clearly and easily highlight and catalogue any prisoner’s previous placement onto the HRATs regime. Response from SA Health •   SA Health’s SA Prison Health Service (SAPHS) are involved in the assessment of prisoners. The admission process is managed by DCS. SAPHS staff are present and rostered at admission sites to conduct assessments as per the DCS Notice of Concern/ High Risk Assessment Team (HRAT) process. SAPHS staff are also part of High Risk Assessment Teams. SAPHS has a procedure for all staff relating to admission assessments. SAPHS nursing staff complete a comprehensive admission assessment document which includes a thorough Mental State Examination. SAPHS record/case notes have all previous HRAT minutes filed. 34 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court SAPHS nursing staff cross reference information with Open Architecture Clinical Information System (OACIS) and Community Based Information System (CBIS) for all admissions. The OACIS application enables real-time access to clinical information across the Adelaide metropolitan public hospitals and CBIS is used across all Adelaide metropolitan mental health services. Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   The Department has made changes to the JIS that were implemented and fully operationalised on 10 December 2018, that now identify that a prisoner is currently subject to HRAT monitoring. The HRAT flag on the JIS has been made more visible to staff members and is clearly visible across a number of JIS screens. Whilst an active HRAT flag is removed once the prisoner is removed from HRAT monitoring, the inactive flag remains on the JIS Warning screen, indicating that the prisoner has previously been subject to HRAT monitoring and the dates that they were subject to that monitoring in the past. This serves as a visual reminder of historical ‘at risk’ periods.

- That the Chief Executive of the Department for Correctional Services mandate that a second Prisoner Stress Screening Form interview be conducted upon completion of the first seven days observation to assess and/or gain further information about the prisoner’s risk of self-harm for the future. An interview should be conducted when a prisoner is proposed to be placed in single cell accommodation that has not been subject to being modified under the safe cells policy, or when transferring to a new Division of a DCS facility or a new facility. Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   7-Day Observation Form is commenced during the prisoner’s induction interview, or within 24-hours of placement in an accommodation unit. This form is completed on a daily basis over the prisoners first seven (7) days in prison, and each time a prisoner is placed in a different accommodation unit within the same prison. It includes information obtained from both the prisoner and from the completing Correctional Officers observations, in order to appropriately flag any issues that may have the potential to lead to prisoner self-harm. A Clinical Working Group recently met to discuss these requirements, resulting in the amendment of the 7 days observation form to include questions regarding stress, suicide and self-harm. Daily observations are to be made with comments recorded appropriately and followed up on as required. An electronic case note must be written at the completion of the 7-day observations. Where a prisoner is transferring between correctional institutions in South Australia, a PSSF is completed upon arrival at the receiving institution, and seven-day observations are commenced. DCS has completed a review into the PSSF. The department has identified it has rigorous processes in place that do not require a second stress screening form due to the current process of seven-day observations, the HRAT intervention services that are available upon admission and the Forensic Mental Health services also available. All officers are trained to identify a prisoner experiencing stress, thoughts of self-harm or suicide and raise a NOC. A Correctional Officer who becomes aware of a prisoner at risk or observes the behaviour or presentation of a prisoner as indicating an increase in risk of suicide or self-harm, must verbally notify the Responsible Officer and must complete a NOC as soon as reasonably possible.

- That all forms needed for the admission of a prisoner, whether in electronic or paper format, be reviewed to improve their ease of use for the correctional officer and the prisoner. 35 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- That the preferred method for admission be by computer records that are easily accessible and formatted. Response from SA Health •   DCS has a hybrid admission system, the Justice Information System (JIS) is a computer-based system and their admission process also includes paper-based documents such as the Prisoner Stress Screening form and the Notice of Concern form. All SAPHS staff have access to the JIS database and can access information on admission. SAPHS can also cross reference information with OACIS and CBIS for all admissions. SAPHS is currently investigating business case options for a SAPHS specific electronic health record. Currently SAPHS only has a paper-based admission record. Response from the Department for Correctional Services for Recommendations 6 and 7 •   DCS has a hybrid admission system, which includes paper-based documents such as the PSSF and the NOC form. White JIS is a computer based system which has some electronic capability for the admission process with the availability of Form F001/004 – Prisoner Interview Form. All prisoner admission forms, including electronic and paper forms are, and will continue to be reviewed in line with the review date for the relevant SOP that the form is associated with. DCS endeavours to ensure all forms requiring staff and/or prisoner input are designed for ease of use whilst ensuring that they cover off on the required information and purpose required under various SOPs. DCS’ new iSAFE offender management system is a major reform initiative aimed at improving security, reducing reoffending and protecting communities by replacing existing ICT legacy systems (Green and White JIS) with a system that will better support effective and holistic end to end case management across corrections from entry to exit. iSAFE will automate the admission process in line with requirements set out in SOP 001. iSAFE will standardise information collection through the use of online forms, aim to capture data once and then reuse it across common data points to reduce manual entry and error, and enable the use of supported and mobile devices to better support the admission process and drive digitisation by default.

Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   When a prisoner with an active HRAT flag is discharged from custody the flag is deactivated, if readmitted, the inactive flag remains visible on the JIS Warning screen, indicating that the prisoner has previously been subject to HRAT monitoring, including the dates that they were subject to that monitoring in the past. Prisoners being admitted or transferred who have a previous HRAT history are not automatically required to be placed on a NOC, however it must be taken into consideration. Officers conducting the induction interview consider active risks during the admissions process, notably, during completion of a PSSF whereby if certain questions are endorsed by the prisoner a NOC must be completed. In addition, a NOC must be completed if the overall PSSF score is eight (8) or more, and/or if the interviewing officer’s assessment is that the prisoner requires further assessment by the HRAT team. Once completed by the interviewing officer, the PSSF is reviewed utilising a checklist and endorsed by the ‘Responsible Officer’ and a ‘tick box’ completed confirming whether a NOC has been completed or not. If the warning flag is active for the admitting prison relating to self-harm or suicide history, JIS automatically generates an email advising of the prisoner’s potential risk. 37 | P a g e OFFICIAL 2021-22 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court This automated email will be forwarded to site staff that are listed within the local HRAT Distribution List (DL). Response from the Department for Correctional Services •   SOP 016 – Prohibited Items and Restricted Materials and its Appendix – Prohibited Items and Restricted Materials is silent on items that have a potential to act as ligatures. All items within DCS institutions undergo a risk assessment prior to their approval to be within their respective institutions. DCS aim to provide a balance between reducing risk and ensuring humane and dignified care as well as progression opportunities to less restrictive more normalised environments. Classifying items that have the potential to act as ligatures is too broad. This would potentially result in items such as clothing and blankets being included. It is acknowledged that each site may have a specific LIS related to items that have a potential to act as a ligature.
